add.label: B.8
add.name: Heavy stacks
add.proof:
Basis extension gives $B^\top\mathbb Z^I=\mathbb Z^d$ for a saturated lattice.
The rank $d$ fiber bound is $m(\Theta)\le g^{-d}$.
Any set $F$ of density at least $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ has $m(F^\perp)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}>g^{-4}$.
Thus its normal lattice has rank at most three.

\emph{Prefix estimates.}

For a saturated rank $d$ lattice on $I$ with basis $B$, order $I$ with a largest minor $J$ first.
Let $I_k$ be the first $k$ indices.
Let $\Theta_k$ be the integer points in the column span of $B_{I_k}$, with height $h_k$ and density $m_k$.
Invertibility gives $\Theta_d=\mathbb Z^J$. Its height is one. Point fibers give $m_d=g^{-d}$.
Saturation gives $\Theta_{|I|}=\Theta$.
For any prefix write $B_{I_k}=YC$ with $Y$ a basis matrix of $\Theta_k$ and $C$ a nonsingular integer matrix.
Every maximal minor of $B_{I_k}$ is the corresponding minor of $Y$ multiplied by $\det C$.
Thus $J$ remains a largest minor.
The fibers of $\Theta_k$ are the level sets of $B_{I_k}^\top$ because $C$ is invertible.
The image $G_k:=B_{I_k}^\top\mathbb Z^{I_k}$ equals $C^\top\mathbb Z^d$ since a saturated basis extends to a basis of the ambient lattice.
Consequently $h_k[\mathbb Z^d:G_k]=h(\Theta)$.
Let $s_k$ be the order of the new row modulo $G_k$.
Adjoining the row enlarges $G_k$ by index $s_k$.
The height identity then gives $h_{k+1}=s_k h_k$.
In a fiber of the next prefix the new coordinate belongs to one residue class modulo $s_k$, since subtracting its row contribution must land in $G_k$.
There are at most $\lceil g/s_k\rceil$ such values in the box, at most one for $s_k\ge g$.
Conditioning on that coordinate gives $m_{k+1}\le m_k\lceil g/s_k\rceil/g$.
For $2\le s_k<g$, this ratio is at most $s_k^{-1+1/b}$: indeed $1+s_k/g\le s_k^{1/b}$.
For $s_k\ge2^b$ the last inequality follows from $1+s_k/g<2$.
The concave function $s^{1/b}-1-s2^{-b}$ vanishes at $2^b$.
The exponential bound gives $2^{1/b}-1\ge(\ln2)/b$.
For $b\ge7$, $(\ln2)/b>2^{1-b}$.
Thus the function is positive at $2$.
Concavity gives the inequality for $2\le s_k\le2^b$ by $g\ge2^b$.
Multiplying the two recursions gives $m_{k+1}^bh_{k+1}^{b-1}\le m_k^bh_k^{b-1}$ for $s_k<g$, including $s_k=1$.

In rank three let $n'$ count the steps with $s_k\ge2$.
The density bound gives $g^3 m(\Theta)\le\prod_{s_k\ge2}(1/s_k+1/g)$.
The product of the $s_k$ is $h(\Theta)$.
The terms with a factor $1/g$ sum to at most $(1/2+1/g)^{n'}-2^{-n'}$ by expansion.
For $n'\ge1$ the mean value theorem bounds this difference by $n'(1/2+1/g)^{n'-1}/g$.
The bound increases from $n'=1$ to $2$.
It decreases thereafter since the successive ratio is at most $(3/2)(1/2+1/g)<1$.
As $\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1+2/g$, this gives $g^3m(\Theta)\le\xi_{\mathrm{tr}}(1/h(\Theta)+1/g)$.
For $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, rearranging yields $h(\Theta)\le H_3$ by (I2).
Multiplying the weakened density inequality by the height gives regularity by (I4).

\emph{Trimming.}
Form $X=\Sigma_\Theta^{-1/2}(B^\top r_I-y_\Theta)$.
Adding independent uniform noise on $[-1/2,1/2]$ to a centered box coordinate makes it uniform on an interval of length $g$.
The noise has moment generating function at least one by Jensen's inequality.
Thus the coordinate's moment generating function is bounded by $\sinh(tg/2)/(tg/2)$.
The series bounds this by $e^{t^2g^2/24}$ since $(2k+1)!\ge6^k k!$.
Independence gives $\mathbb E e^{u^\top X}\le e^{\|u\|^2/2}$.

For an independent standard Gaussian $Z$ in dimension $d$, integrating over $Z$ gives
$\mathbb E e^{99\|X\|^2/200}=\mathbb E e^{\sqrt{99/100}Z^\top X}$.
Integrating over $X$ first bounds the latter expectation by $\mathbb E e^{99\|Z\|^2/200}$.
The Gaussian square moment formula evaluates this as $10^d$.
Markov's inequality bounds the trimming loss by $10^d e^{-99R_{\mathrm{tr}}^2/200}$.
This is at most $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by (I2).

\emph{Counting trimmed images.}
Take $F$ on $I\cup\{i'\}$ trimmed by a rank $d$ lattice $\Theta$ on $I$.
Fibers of $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_I,r_{i'})$ have density at most $m(\Theta)/g$ by independence.
For full image dimension $k=d+1$ and coset index $q$, set $\delta=q$.
For the lower-dimensional estimate assume that $F^\perp$ has rank $1\le d'<d$, with a largest minor at $J\subseteq I$, and its restrictions to $I$ lie in the span of $\Theta$.
Put $k=d+1-d'$.
The rows $B_J$ have rank $d'$ since their column span contains the invertible minor of a basis of $F^\perp$.
Choose the final $k-1$ columns $B_2$ of $B$ to vanish on $J$, by extending an integer basis of the saturated kernel of $B_J$ to an integer basis of $\mathbb Z^d$.
Under a unimodular basis change $B\mapsto BU$, the centered image is multiplied by $U^\top$.
Its shape matrix becomes $U^\top\Sigma_\Theta U$.
Unimodularity preserves the absolute maximal minors.
Invertibility of $U^\top$ preserves the fibers.
Substitution preserves the ellipsoid inequality.
Write $B_1$ for the other columns.
The map $a\mapsto(Ba_{[d]},a_{d+1})$ takes the real normal space of $\Phi(F)$ isomorphically to that of $F$, by the hypothesis on restrictions.
Thus the image has affine dimension $k$.
If $V$ is a basis matrix of $\Phi(F)^\perp$, split it into row blocks $V_1,V_2,V_3$ with $d',k-1,1$ rows.
The mapped basis generates a full-rank sublattice of $F^\perp$. Its minor at $J$ gives $|\det(B_1)_J|\,|\det V_1|\ge h(F^\perp)$.
Projection dropping the first $d'$ coordinates is injective on the image, since $V_1$ is invertible and differences satisfy $V^\top y=0$.
Write $(y_2,x)$ for the retained coordinates, with $x$ last. Projected differences vanish under $(y_2,x)\mapsto V_2^\top y_2+V_3^\top x$ modulo $V_1^\top\mathbb Z^{d'}$.
This map onto the quotient is surjective by saturation of the normal lattice.
Thus the projected coset has index $\delta:=|\det V_1|$.

In either case the $k$-dimensional projected cylinder has volume $(g-1)\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb B^{k-1})R_{\mathrm{tr}}^{k-1}(g^2/12)^{(k-1)/2}\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}$, by the ellipsoid projection formula.
Here $\mathbb B^{k-1}$ is the unit ball. For full dimension use $B_2=B$ with empty $J$ and $B_1$.
The image contains a simplex of volume at least $\delta/k!$ by the coset determinant.
Blichfeldt bounds the count by $k!$ times the cylinder volume divided by $\delta$, plus $k$.
The simplex bound absorbs $k$ into $(k+1)!$ times the scaled volume.
By Cauchy--Binet, $|\det (B_1)_J|\sqrt{\det(B_2^\top B_2)}\le h(\Theta)\sqrt{\binom N{k-1}}$, since each product of minors is a minor of $B$ by $(B_2)_J=0$.
Use $g-1\le g$ and $\binom N{k-1}\le N^{k-1}/(k-1)!$ in the volume bound.
The factors $(k+1)!\operatorname{vol}(\mathbb B^{k-1})R_{\mathrm{tr}}^{k-1}(N/12)^{(k-1)/2}/\sqrt{(k-1)!}$ are at most $\Lambda_{k-1}$ for $k-1=1,2,3$, by the unit ball volumes and (I3).
Multiplying the count by the fiber density bound yields $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_dg^dh(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$ in full dimension.
In the other case multiply by $h(F^\perp)\le\delta |\det(B_1)_J|$ to get $\Pr[F]h(F^\perp)\le\Lambda_{d-d'}g^{d-d'}h(\Theta)m(\Theta)$.

\emph{Regularizing a dense lattice.}
For a rank $d$ saturated lattice of density at least $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$, we show that a regular saturated superlattice loses at most $(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ in density.
Induct downwards from rank three, where the prefix estimate already gives regularity.
For $d<3$ use the prefix order with largest minor first.
The prefix densities are nonincreasing by the density recursion.
Take successively a densest prefix fiber $F_k$, trimming it by $\tilde\Theta_{k-1}$ if the preceding normal lattice exceeded the preceding prefix.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F_k]\ge m_k-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $F_k^\perp$ exceeds $\Theta_k$, its rank is at least $d+1$ by saturation.
Its rank is at most three by the density bound.
Its density meets the induction threshold $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-\operatorname{rank}F_k^\perp)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $m_k\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The induction gives a regular superlattice $\tilde\Theta_k$ with density at least $m_k-(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If this promotion occurs at the final prefix, use that superlattice.

Otherwise let $j$ be the last promoted prefix, or $d-1$ if none was promoted.
For $j<k<|I|$, if $s_k\ge g$ then the next coordinate is constant on $F_{k+1}$.
Its unit vector then belongs to $F_{k+1}^\perp=\Theta_{k+1}$.
It vanishes on $J$, contradicting invertibility.
Thus $s_k<g$.
The prefix power inequality bounds $m(\Theta)^b h(\Theta)^{b-1}$ by $m_{j+1}^b h_{j+1}^{b-1}$.
It suffices to bound the latter by $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}(\Gamma_d/g^d)^{b-1}$, since $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
If $j=d-1$, this is the initial height and density bound together with (I4).
Otherwise let $\tilde d$ be the rank of $\tilde\Theta_j$.
The normal lattice of $F_{j+1}$ is $\Theta_{j+1}$, with largest minor at $J$.
Its restriction lies in the span of $\Theta_j\subseteq\tilde\Theta_j$.
Thus the lower-dimensional estimate applies to $F_{j+1}$ trimmed by $\tilde\Theta_j$.
By regularity of $\tilde\Theta_j$ the estimate gives $\Pr[F_{j+1}]h_{j+1}\le\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}/g^d$.
By (I4), $m_{j+1}\le A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Pr[F_{j+1}]$ because $\Pr[F_{j+1}]\ge m_{j+1}-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ and $m_{j+1}\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

Monotonicity gives $m_{j+1}\le m_j$.
Trimming gives $m_j\le\Pr[F_j]+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The promoted normal rank bounds $\Pr[F_j]\le g^{-d-1}$.
Now (I4) gives $m_{j+1}\le\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}P_d^{b-1}$.
Multiplying these estimates gives
\[
m_{j+1}^b h_{j+1}^{b-1}\le\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}(A_{\mathrm{inv}}\Lambda_{\tilde d-d}\Gamma_{\tilde d}P_d/g^d)^{b-1}.
\]
This is the required bound by (I4).
Thus the original lattice is regular in this case.

\emph{The modular fiber.}

For a nonzero $v$ with $v_0=0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$, omit coordinate zero and the zero entries to obtain $v_1,\ldots,v_{N_0}$.
Conditioning on the coordinates after a prefix bounds the full guessing probability by that of the prefix.
We inductively find a regular saturated lattice $\Theta$ of density $m(\Theta)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ whose reduction contains $v_{[i]}$.
For $i=1$, use $\mathbb Z$, whose density $1/g$ is that of the densest modular fiber by injectivity on the box.
The existence of a prefix fiber above $\theta$ shows $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<1/g$.
Now $\Gamma_1\ge1$ follows from (I4).
Thus the initial lattice of height one is regular.
A rank $d$ lattice from the induction has height at most $H_d$ by regularity for $d\le2$ and the rank-three bound otherwise.

Restriction to a largest minor $J$ gives a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)$.
The cited successive minima and basis bound on this lattice gives a basis there with product of $\ell_1$ norms at most $h(\Theta)$, $2h(\Theta)$ or $9h(\Theta)$ in ranks one, two or three.
Lift this basis to the columns of $B$.
By Cramer's rule every coordinate on the column span is a linear combination of the coordinates in $J$ with coefficients of magnitude at most one, since each replaced minor is bounded by the largest minor.
Thus the $\ell_1$ norms on $J$ bound the full column infinity norms.

Write $v_{[i]}=Bc'$ modulo $q$.
For the next prefix take a densest modular fiber trimmed by $\Theta$, denoted by $F$.
Trimming gives $\Pr[F]>\theta-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Under $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_{[i]},r_{i+1})$ its image lies in a coset of index $q$, by the congruence with coefficients $c=(c',v_{i+1})$.
In full dimension the trimmed image bound gives $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_dg^dh(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$.
Regularity bounds this by $\Lambda_d\Gamma_d/q$.
Condition (I5) makes this smaller than $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Thus the affine dimension is at most $d$.
Let $\Delta$ be the matrix of differences of image points.
In row $j\le d$ its entries are bounded by $T_{\mathrm{tr}}\|Be_j\|_\infty$ by Cauchy--Schwarz in the ellipsoid metric and $|I|\le N$.
Last-row differences are at most $g-1<T_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The determinant expansion bounds its nonzero maximal minors by $d!T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d\prod_j\|Be_j\|_\infty$, since the rank is at most $d$ and each row bound is at least one.
This is below $q$ by the basis and height bounds and (I5).
The rank of $\Delta$ is preserved modulo $q$, since a nonzero maximal minor is below $q$.
In Smith normal form this means that every nonzero invariant factor is invertible modulo $q$.
Hence any modular left null vector lifts to an integer left null vector, by setting the constrained coordinates in Smith coordinates to zero and lifting the free coordinates.
Apply this to $c$ to choose $u$ in the integer left kernel with $u\equiv c\bmod q$.
Then $(Bu_{[d]},u_{d+1})$ belongs to $F^\perp$, by pulling the constant functional on $\Phi(F)$ back through $\Phi$.
Its reduction is $v_{[i+1]}$.
Its normal rank is at most three by the density bound.
Its rank is positive since it contains a lift of $v_{[i+1]}$.
By the definition of $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $m(F^\perp)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Regularization supplies the next lattice containing $F^\perp$, with density loss at most $2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.

In the final lattice choose $z_0\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $Bz_0\equiv v_{[N_0]}\bmod q$.
The integer vectors congruent to multiples of $z_0$ form an index $q^{d-1}$ sublattice because $z_0$ is nonzero modulo $q$.
Its image under $B_J$, for a largest minor $J$, has determinant $h(\Theta)q^{d-1}$.
By (I6) this determinant is at most $\beta^d/d!$, using the integer height bound $\lfloor H_3\rfloor$ in rank three.
Minkowski's theorem in the closed $\ell_1$ ball of radius $\beta$ gives a nonzero point $B_Jz$ of this image.
The coordinate bound gives $\|Bz\|_\infty\le\beta$.
The reduction of $Bz$ is nonzero since $B_Jz\ne0$ and $\beta<q$.
It is a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$ by the choice of the sublattice.
Restore the deleted coordinates as zeros to get $x$.

\emph{Application to heavy stacks.}

Choose a column basis of the matrix of stacked rows, including column zero if nonzero.
Fixing the other coordinates, each fiber specifies at most one tuple at the basis coordinates.
On the basis coordinates in $[N]$ such a tuple has probability $g^{-1}$ per coordinate by independence and uniformity.
If coordinate zero is in the basis, the remaining prescribed residue has conditional probability at most $1/g$ given all other coordinates, by the uniform choice of $r_\star$.
For the independent sampler this last bound follows from the uniform choice of $r_0$.
Consequently a rank of at least four would bound the probability of every fiber by $g^{-4}<\theta$.
For $v$ in the row space, each fiber of the stack is contained in a fiber of $v^\top$, since $v^\top r$ is a linear function of the stack times $r$.
Thus $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$.
A kernel vector satisfies $v_0=0$ by the form $\varphi_0$.
The modular fiber argument above supplies its short multiple under (P3).
Any short multiple reduces to a nonzero vector in the kernel, by linearity.
Its coordinate zero is zero as an integer by $\beta<q$.
The remaining forms are precisely the coefficients of $A\hat x$ by the definition of the forms.
Packing keeps all coordinates $1,\ldots,N$ and adds zeros, so the packed norm equals the positive norm of $x$.
add.statement: Under (P3), a heavy stack has rank at most three. Every kernel vector in its row space has a short multiple. A short multiple $x$ of any kernel vector packs into an MSIS solution $\hat x$ for the columns $1,\ldots,\ell$ of $M$, with $0<\|\hat x\|_\infty\le\beta$ and $A\hat x=0$ modulo $q$.

add.label: B.16
add.name: Extractor
add.proof:
First take a nonzero usable stack with row space $\mathcal V$ of dimension at most three and no kernel vector. Let $\mathcal U$ have columns a basis of $\mathcal V$, with rows $u_i$.
Let $d$ count the basis columns.
Form $h_s=\mathcal U^\top\sigma^s(z)$ for every integer $s$.
The coordinates of $h_0$ are independent over $\mathbb F_q$ since $z$ has zero kernel on $\mathcal V$.
The entries of $h_{n/2-1}$ remain base-field independent under Frobenius. Its first $d$ consecutive conjugates form an invertible Moore matrix.
Apply a left inverse of $\mathcal U$ on the left and its transpose on the right of $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ to obtain $\Xi_s$ at $s=n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1$, respectively. Congruence preserves symmetry.
Multiplication by $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal U^\top$ recovers each matrix by its column and row spaces.
The ties modulo $P$ give $\Xi_s h_{s'}=\Xi_{s'}h_s$.
If $\sum_s\varrho_s h_s=0$, the matrix $\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s$ kills each $h_{s'}$ by the ties.
It is therefore zero by spanning.
Thus there is a linear map $\Xi(h_s)=\Xi_s$.
The form $\Xi(h;u,u')=u^\top\Xi(h)u'$ is symmetric in $u,u'$ by symmetry of the matrices.
The ties give symmetry in $h,u'$ by spanning.
Booleanity gives $\Xi(h;u_j,u_j-u_0)=0$ for all $h$, since it holds at the three $h_s$ by linearity of the tests on the cells.
Also $\Xi_s=\sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ at $s=n/2-1,n/2$ by conjugation of the coefficient matrices and the even powers of $W_V$.

If $u_0=0$, choose basis rows $u_j$ of $\mathcal U$.
Every tensor entry with a repeated basis row vanishes by Booleanity and symmetry.
For $d<3$ this makes the stack zero.
For $d=3$ only the common entry $t$ on triples of distinct basis rows can survive.
The conjugate identities on the off-diagonal entries in this basis give $t h_s=\sigma^s(t)h_0$ at $s=n/2-1,n/2$.
In dimension three the first two conjugates are independent as columns of that Moore matrix.
Thus $t=0$, contradicting a nonzero stack.

Extend $u_0$ to a basis of rows at indices $J$.
For $\delta\in\{0,1\}^{J\setminus\{0\}}$, choose $p_\delta$ with $u_0^\top p_\delta=1$ and $u_j^\top p_\delta=\delta_j$ at the other basis indices.
Booleanity and symmetry make each tensor entry on basis rows depend only on the set $A$ of distinct nonzero indices in its triple, since a repeated nonzero index can be replaced once by zero.
The cubes of the $p_\delta$ have entries $\prod_{k\in A}\delta_k$ at such triples.
These monomials form a basis of functions on the Boolean cube, by the triangular subset incidence matrix.
Hence $\Xi(h)=\sum_\delta c_\delta(h^\top p_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
The squares $p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ are also independent since every subset $A$ occurs in a pair of basis rows for $d\le3$.
Form $w_\delta=\mathcal U p_\delta$.
Then $z(w_\delta)\ne0$ by the kernel hypothesis.
Comparing square coefficients shows that both conjugations fix $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)$.
Their consecutive powers generate $\sigma$.
Thus $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)\in\mathbb F_q$.

For a passing test $\varrho$, put $\mathcal Q=\sum_\delta\frac{c_\delta}{z(w_\delta)}\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
The test vanishes on $W_U$ and $W_V$ by linearity on the cells.
It vanishes on $\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ by base-field linearity under conjugation.
Substitution gives $h_0^\top\mathcal Qh_s=0$ for the three conjugate indices.
Spanning gives $h_0^\top\mathcal Q=0$.
The field independence of the coordinates of $h_0$ gives $\mathcal Q=0$, since $\mathcal Q$ has base-field entries.
Independence of the squares gives $\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)=0$ whenever $c_\delta\ne0$.
At least one coefficient is nonzero since $W_U,W_V$ determine the stack.
For such a coefficient, Booleanity gives $(w_\delta)_j((w_\delta)_j-1)=0$ at each coordinate $j\in[N]$.
Each constraint test on $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ gives its constraint on $w_\delta$ by substitution into the test.
Since $(w_\delta)_0=1$, this is a witness in $\mathcal V$.

\emph{The extractor tests.}

Each candidate is checked against $S$ before output.
Up to the first mark, records represent monitor entries with guess variables set to zero, up to formal equality.
Indeed an unseen valid operand is a guess, represented by zero.
The substitution of zero commutes with the operations on expressions.
The monitor keeps only formally equal expressions at a label before the first mark.
The view result for a formally zero difference gives $W_c r=u_c$ at every $r$.
Varying $r$ forces each $W_c$ to vanish.
Thus formally equal expressions have equal stacks.

At a good key mark the entry is a result, since it contains no guess variable and received target-group elements have zero stacks.
Hence its sketches are tested.
At a good difference mark, the old entry has a record by the time the result is tested.
Indeed, a guess that has never been an answered operand cannot cancel from the difference unless it is an operand of the current call.
Thus the tested difference has the mark stack, by linearity and the record invariant.

Fix a run with a good first mark and no kernel vector in the mark row space.
Its stack is usable by the view result. Its row space has dimension at most three by the heavy stack bound.
Symmetry makes the image of $(v_c)_c\mapsto\sum_c W_c v_c$ the row space.
Conditional on the run, the independent probes give three independent uniform images in the row space.
Their span equals the row space except with probability at most $2/q$.
That row space contains a witness by the preceding tied-form argument.
A witness is among the tested candidates because coordinate zero is a pivot for any space with a vector having a nonzero coordinate zero.
If a witness was already returned before these tests, extraction has already succeeded.
Averaging over runs proves the probability bound.

\emph{The reductions.}
At a uniform challenge the programmed entries are jointly uniform. The remaining oracle entries are sampled independently in (R1).
Exchangeability of unused labels and exponents gives the uniform injection law.
Thus (R1) has the law of the run with message $m_b$.
The coins of (R2) are independent of this run.

At a good key mark, (R3) takes the target record.
It represents $\mathsf D$ up to formal equality by the record invariant.
At a good difference mark, the analogous record difference represents $\mathsf D$.
Before the first mark, equal-label records have formally equal expressions by the invariant.
Thus no earlier difference is detected.
In the difference case $\mathsf D$ is formally nonzero by (M3).
The degree bound applies to $\varpi\operatorname{val}(\mathsf D)$.
This polynomial is nonzero since $\mathsf D$ is formally nonzero.
On valid coins $\varpi\ne0$ by its factors.
The coordinate $\tau$ excludes $D$ values.
The coordinate $\varepsilon$ excludes at most $K_1+1\le D$.
Every other coin excludes at most one value.
Schwartz--Zippel bounds private evaluation failure by $d_f/(q-D)\le\varepsilon_f$.

By the encryption formula, $\kappa$ depends on neither $r$ nor $\alpha$.
For a good mark, compare the affine identity's coefficients in $\alpha$, which ranges over more than one value.
The plain expression is identically $\chi\kappa$ at $r$.
The alpha pairing terms with the copy indices removed give an expression identically $-\mathsf D_K\kappa$ at $r$.
These values are affine in $r$ by the right exponent formulas.
The view locus makes each value constant on its sector's stack fiber.
Its gradient thus annihilates that stack's kernel.
The gradient lies in the row space by duality.
In particular the plain gradient vanishes when the mark uses the alpha sector.
Formally equal expressions have equal affine functions of $r$. Their derivatives therefore coincide.

For each point, keep $\pi,s_{\mathrm X},\upsilon,y,\varepsilon,\Omega_{12},\zeta''$ random and fix the other coins.
In the sector gradient after removing the common sector factor, the coefficient of $\pi s_{\mathrm X}\upsilon^{k_c}y_i$ is the row $W_{c,i}$.
Only the first right coordinates contain $r$ by the published formulas.
Their derivatives after removing the sector factor have the single coefficient $s_{\mathrm{leg}}$.
A second left factor's term in $y_i$ contains $\Omega_{12}$.
The cancellation column has $\zeta''$ instead of $\pi$.
The cell is identified by $(\mathrm X,k_c)$ in the constant part in $\varepsilon$.
The factor contributions have degree at most $k_c+5$ from two scalars, their powers, $\varepsilon$, $y_i$ and $\Omega_{12}$.
The other left coordinates contribute degree at most $k_{\mathrm{leg}}+3$ by their formulas.
Thus the gradient has degree at most $n+4$.
Choose a basis of mark-stack rows of size $d$. Project to a nonzero $d$-column minor of these rows.
The determinant of the first $d$ projected vectors has this minor as the coefficient of the product of the selected monomials at the separate points.
Its degree is at most $d(n+4)$.
Schwartz--Zippel bounds failure to span by $d(n+4)/(q-D)$.
This is at most $\varepsilon_f$ since $d\le3$ and $n\le D$.

On both successes, (R5) finds a kernel vector since the recovered row space is the mark row space.
The heavy-stack result supplies a short multiple.
The lifting algorithm returns one.
Packing gives an MSIS solution.
Any earlier successful output also solves MSIS because (R5) uses a kernel vector and a short multiple.
Conditional on each such run, the two failures cost at most $2\varepsilon_f$ by the union bound.
Success over uniform challenges has probability $s_b$ by its definition.
Adding the failure bound proves the good-mark estimate.

\emph{Reduction time.}
Evaluate received exponents at eight points.
Program $k\ell$ seed entries.
Both $K_1,K_2\le n$ by $K_1K_2=n/2$.
The form ranges are bounded by $n=(k+1)d_R$.
The chunk ranges are $O(D)$ by (P1) and the definitions of the lengths.
Thus the published formulas give polynomial initialization cost in $D,\log q$.
QAP coefficients need $O(ND)$ advice.
Message advice has length at most $\mu$.
Masking costs $O(\mu)$.
Each generic call updates the label and exponent tables at constant cost per point.
The value comparison at the private point implements the difference test of (R3).
The target record is a table lookup.
Seed queries cost $O(d_R)$ each by lazy sampling.
Key queries cost constant work in the stipulated model.

There are $O(Q+L)$ circuit nodes since each call contributes a bounded number.
Use the actual operation coefficients as circuit constants. Zero the other-sector inputs.

For the run with message $m_b$ and uniform $M$, a good first mark with a row-space kernel vector has probability at most $s_b+2\varepsilon_f$. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.9, if $\mathcal A$ runs in time $t$ and makes at most $Q_H$ queries to each random oracle, each reduction runs in time $t_R=t+O(Q+d_R Q_H+\mu)+\mathsf{poly}(D,\log q)$, with description and advice included.

add.name: QAP criterion
add.statement: For admissible evaluation points and symmetric $W$, the tests pass exactly when $P_W=h'Z+Z_0R$ with $R$ allowed and $\deg h'<D$. Equivalently, $P_W-W_{00}L_\rho=h(X)Z(X)(X-\rho)+Z_0R$ with $R$ allowed and $\deg h<D-1$. In either identity $R=R_W$.
add.proof:
Both division numerators agree on the roots of $Z$ because $L_\rho$ vanishes there.
At $\rho$ its corrected value is $W_{00}-W_{00}=0$ by evaluation.
Thus both divisibilities impose exactly the vanishing conditions at the roots of $Z$.
At $d_0$ vanishing is automatic.
At $d_j$ for $j\in[N]$ it is the Booleanity test.
At the coset points it forces $R=R_W$ by interpolation.
The coset sum formula gives a Vandermonde matrix on the coefficients at exponents divisible by $\nu$, with distinct entries $\delta_t^\nu$ as evaluation points.
The sum vector vanishes exactly when these coefficients vanish by invertibility and $\nu\ne0$ in the field.
By the QAP table these sums are precisely the constraint tests.
Thus either required division exists exactly when $W$ passes.
Both numerators have degree at most $2D-2$ by the input degrees.
Dividing by the degree $D-1$ or degree $D$ polynomial gives the claimed bounds.

add.label: B.2
add.name: Convex interpolation
add.proof:
The quadratic coefficient of $E$ is nonnegative by its formula.
Hence $E$ is convex.
Condition (P5) gives $E(2)\le2^{-\lambda}$.
Adding its two inequalities gives $E(2^{\lambda+1})\le1$.
Convex interpolation gives $E(u)\le u/2^{\lambda+1}$ between the endpoints.
Take $u=2Q+2$.
